modern: Good old Jacob could no longer be with Joseph, for his hour to die had come; but he left his son without anxiety, for he said with confidence, “God shall be with you.” When our dearest relatives or our most helpful friends are called home by death, we must comfort ourselves with the thought that the Lord hasn’t left us, but lives for us and stays with us forever.

If God is with us, we are in noble company, even if we are poor and despised. If God is with us, we have all-sufficient strength, for nothing can be too hard for the Lord. If God is with us, we are always safe, for no one can harm those who walk under his shadow. Oh, what joy we have here! God is not only with us, but he will be with us: with us as individuals, with us as families, with us as churches. Isn’t the very name of Jesus Immanuel, God with us? Isn’t this the best of all, that God is with us? Let’s be bravely hard-working and joyfully hopeful. Our cause must prosper, the truth must win, for the Lord is with those who are with him.
All through this day may this sweet word be enjoyed by every believer who turns to “Faith’s Check Book.” No greater happiness is possible.

notes.note: The dying Jacob to his son Joseph ([[Gen.48.21|Genesis 48:21]]).
Raising us up; making us noble.

notes.term: Nothing can be too hard for the Lord
notes.note: “Is any thing too hard for the LORD?” ([[Gen.18.14|Genesis 18:14]]).
“He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty” ([[Ps.91.1|Psalm 91:1]]).
“God with us” ([[Matt.1.23|Matthew 1:23]]).
Spurgeon’s own title for this book (1888): each promise is like a check that faith can cash at the bank of heaven.

modern: Ours isn’t a life of anxious care, but of happy faith. Our heavenly Father will supply the needs of his own children, and he knows what we need before we ask him. So we can go to bed at a sensible hour, and not wear ourselves out sitting up late to plot and plan and scheme. If we have learned to rely on our God, we won’t lie awake with fear gnawing at our hearts. We will leave our care with the Lord, our thoughts of him will be sweet, and he will give us refreshing sleep.

To be loved by the Lord is the highest honor possible, and whoever has it may feel that ambition itself could want nothing more, and so every selfish wish may go to sleep. What more is there, even in heaven, than the love of God? Rest, then, my soul, for you have everything.

Yet we toss and turn unless the Lord himself gives us not only the reasons for rest but rest itself. And he does. Jesus himself is our peace, our rest, our all. On his breast we sleep in perfect security, in life and in death.

notes.term: He knoweth what we have need of
notes.note: “For your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him” ([[Matt.6.8|Matthew 6:8]]).
The verse before the text: “It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows” ([[Ps.127.2|Psalm 127:2]]).

notes.term: Our meditation of Him shall be sweet
notes.note: “My meditation of him shall be sweet: I will be glad in the LORD” ([[Ps.104.34|Psalm 104:34]]).
Those God loves: “for so he giveth his beloved sleep.”
“For he is our peace” ([[Eph.2.14|Ephesians 2:14]]).
The chest, the place of closest embrace.

modern: We need a guide. Sometimes we would give everything we have to be told exactly what to do and which way to turn. We are willing to do right, but we don’t know which of two roads to take. Oh, for a guide!

The Lord our God stoops to be our guide. He knows the way, and will pilot us along it until we reach our journey’s end in peace. Surely we couldn’t want more unfailing direction. Let’s put ourselves completely under his guidance, and we will never lose our way. Let’s make him our God, and we will find him our guide. If we follow his law we won’t miss the right road of life, provided we first learn to lean on him in every step we take.

Our comfort is that, since he is our God forever and ever, he will never stop being with us as our guide. He will lead us “even unto death,” and then we will live with him eternally and go out no more forever. This promise of divine guidance includes lifelong security: salvation at once, guidance to our last hour, and then endless happiness. Shouldn’t everyone seek this in youth, rejoice in it in middle age and rest in it in old age? Today let’s look up for guidance before we trust ourselves out of doors.

notes.note: Stoops down to help, in the good sense, without today’s sense of looking down on someone.
Never wrong; never failing.

notes.term: Go no more out for ever
notes.note: “Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out” ([[Rev.3.12|Revelation 3:12]]).
Rest.

modern: If God willed it, we could live without bread, as Jesus did for forty days; but we couldn’t live without his Word. By that Word we were created, and by it alone can we be kept in being, for he upholds all things by the word of his power. Bread is a second cause; the Lord himself is the first source of our nourishment. He can work without the second cause as well as with it, and we mustn’t tie him down to one way of working. Let’s not be too eager for the visible, but look to the invisible God. We have heard believers say that in deep poverty, when bread ran short, their appetites grew short too; and to others, when ordinary supplies failed, the Lord has sent unexpected help. But we must have the Word of the Lord. With it alone we can stand against the devil. Take it from us, and our enemy will have us in his power, for we will soon faint. Our souls need food, and there is none for them outside the Word of the Lord. All the books and all the preachers in the world can’t supply us with a single meal; only the Word from the mouth of God can fill the mouth of a believer. Lord, give us this bread forevermore. We value it above a king’s delicacies.

notes.term: Man shall not live by bread alone
notes.note: Jesus’ answer to the devil after fasting forty days in the wilderness ([[Matt.4.2-Matt.4.4|Matthew 4:2–4]]), quoting [[Deut.8.3|Deuteronomy 8:3]].

notes.term: He sustaineth all things by the Word of His power
notes.note: “Upholding all things by the word of his power” ([[Heb.1.3|Hebrews 1:3]]).
An ordinary means God works through, such as bread for hunger. God himself is the first cause behind them all.

notes.term: Lord, evermore give us this bread

notes.note: A king’s delicacies.

modern: When the Lord’s faithful ones are suffering for him, they will have sweet messages of love from him, and sometimes they will have good news for those who sympathize with them and help them. Ebed-melech was only a despised Ethiopian, but he was kind to Jeremiah, and so the Lord sent him this special promise by the mouth of his prophet. Let’s always remember God’s persecuted servants, and he will reward us.

Ebed-melech was to be rescued from the men whose revenge he feared. He was a humble Black man, but Jehovah would take care of him. Thousands were killed by the Chaldeans, but this lowly African couldn’t be harmed. We too may be afraid of some powerful people who are bitter against us; but if we have been faithful to the Lord’s cause in the hour of persecution, he will be faithful to us. After all, what can anyone do without the Lord’s permission? He puts a bit in the mouth of rage and a bridle on the head of power. Let’s fear the Lord, and we will have no one else to fear. No cup of cold water given to a despised prophet of God will go without its reward; and if we stand up for Jesus, Jesus will stand up for us.

notes.note: An Ethiopian official in King Zedekiah’s palace who pulled Jeremiah out of the muddy cistern where he had been left to die ([[Jer.38.7-Jer.38.13|Jeremiah 38:7–13]]).
The personal name of God in the Old Testament, printed “the LORD” in most English Bibles.
The Babylonians, who captured Jerusalem.
The ordinary word in Spurgeon’s day for a Black African; it is now dated and offensive.

notes.term: A bit into the mouth of rage
notes.note: “Because thy rage against me… is come up into mine ears, therefore will I put my hook in thy nose, and my bridle in thy lips” ([[Isa.37.29|Isaiah 37:29]]), God’s word to the king of Assyria.
“And whosoever shall give to drink unto one of these little ones a cup of cold water only… he shall in no wise lose his reward” ([[Matt.10.42|Matthew 10:42]]).

modern: Of all the stars in the sky, the North Star is the most useful to the sailor. This text is a North Star, for it has guided more souls to salvation than any other Scripture. It is among the promises what the Great Bear is among the constellations.

Several words in it shine with special brilliance. Here we have God’s love, with a “so” attached, which marks its measureless greatness. Then we have God’s gift, in all its freeness and greatness. This gift is God’s Son, the unique and priceless gift of a love that could never fully show itself until heaven’s only Son had been sent to live and die for men. These three points are full of light.

Then there is the simple requirement of believing, which graciously points to a way of salvation suited to guilty people. This is backed by a wide description: “whosoever believeth in him.” Many have found room in “whosoever” who would have felt shut out by a narrower word. Then comes the great promise, that believers in Jesus will not perish, but have everlasting life. This cheers everyone who feels that he is about to perish and can’t save himself. We believe in the Lord Jesus, and we have eternal life.

notes.note: The North Star, which stays fixed in the sky and was the sailor’s guide.
The constellation that includes the Big Dipper, whose two pointer stars lead the eye to the North Star.
Special, belonging particularly to someone (not odd).
Only, unique: God’s one and only Son.
About to perish.

modern: The comforts of the Lord are so sweet that not only may the saints themselves sing of them, but even the heavens and the earth may take up the song. It takes something to make a mountain sing; and yet the prophet calls together a whole choir of them. Lebanon and Sirion, and the high hills of Bashan and Moab: he would set them all singing because of Jehovah’s grace to his own Zion. Can’t we too make mountains of difficulty and trial and mystery and labor into occasions for praise to our God? “Break forth into singing, O mountains!”

This word of promise, that our God will have mercy on his afflicted, has a whole peal of bells attached to it. Listen to their music: “Sing!” “Be joyful!” “Break forth into singing.” The Lord wants his people happy because of his unfailing love. He doesn’t want us sad and doubtful; he claims from us the worship of believing hearts. He can’t fail us, so why should we sigh or sulk as if he would? Oh, for a well-tuned harp! Oh, for voices like those of the cherubim before the throne!

notes.note: Another name for Mount Hermon ([[Deut.3.9|Deuteronomy 3:9]]). “Lebanon and Sirion like a young unicorn” is from [[Ps.29.6|Psalm 29:6]].
“An high hill as the hill of Bashan” ([[Ps.68.15|Psalm 68:15]]).
The personal name of God in the Old Testament, printed “the LORD” in most English Bibles.
The hill in Jerusalem where the temple stood; here a picture of God’s people.
A full set of church bells rung together.
The mighty angels who stand about God’s throne.

modern: We can’t see the angels, but it is enough that they can see us. There is one great Angel of the Covenant, whom we love though we have not seen him, and his eye is always on us, day and night. He has an army of holy ones under him, and he sets them to watch over his saints and guard them from all harm. If devils do us mischief, shining ones do us service. Notice that the Lord of angels doesn’t come and go, paying us passing visits; he and his armies camp around us. The headquarters of the army of salvation is wherever those live whose trust is in the living God. This camp surrounds the faithful, so that they can’t be attacked from any side unless the enemy can break through the defenses of the Lord of angels. We have a fixed protection, a permanent guard. With God’s messengers as our sentries, we won’t be caught by sudden attacks or swallowed up by overwhelming forces. This verse promises deliverance, deliverance by the great Captain of our salvation, and we will receive it again and again until our warfare is over and we exchange the battlefield for the home of rest.

notes.note: Camps.
Christ, from “the messenger of the covenant” ([[Mal.3.1|Malachi 3:1]]).

notes.term: Whom not having seen we love
notes.note: “Whom having not seen, ye love” ([[1Pet.1.8|1 Peter 1:8]]).
John Bunyan’s name in *The Pilgrim’s Progress* for angels.
Passing, brief.
Guarded by sentries.

notes.term: The great Captain of our salvation
notes.note: [[Heb.2.10|Hebrews 2:10]].
“Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem, and cry unto her, that her warfare is accomplished” ([[Isa.40.2|Isaiah 40:2]]).

modern: If David spoke like this, we can be sure the Son of David is of the same mind. Jesus looks out for faithful people and fixes his eyes on them: to watch them, to bring them forward, to encourage them and to reward them. Let no true-hearted man think he is overlooked; the King himself has his eye on him.

This royal notice has two results. First we read, “that they may dwell with me.” Jesus brings the faithful into his house; he sets them in his palace; he makes them his companions; he delights in their company. We must be true to our Lord, and then he will show himself to us. When our faithfulness costs us most, it will be best rewarded; the more fiercely people reject us, the more joyfully our Lord will receive us.

Next, he says of the sincere man, “he shall serve me.” Jesus will use for his own glory those who scorn the tricks of expediency and are faithful to himself, his Word and his cross. These will be in his royal train, the honored servants of His Majesty. Fellowship and usefulness are the wages of faithfulness. Lord, make me faithful, so that I may live with you and serve you.

notes.note: Jesus, descended from King David ([[Matt.1.1|Matthew 1:1]]).
In the Bible, a blameless, wholehearted way of life rather than a flawless one.
Company.
“He that loveth me… I will love him, and will manifest myself to him” ([[John.14.21|John 14:21]]).
Crafty scheming; doing whatever seems to pay.
The attendants who travel with a king.
Close fellowship and sharing, with God or with each other.

modern: Yes, our prayers for the church will be heard. The set time has come. We love the prayer meeting and the Sunday school and all the services of the Lord’s house. Our hearts are bound to all God’s people, and we can truly say, “There’s not a lamb in all thy flock I would disdain to feed; There’s not a foe before whose face I’d fear thy cause to plead.”

If this is how we generally feel, we will soon enjoy times of refreshing from the presence of the Lord. Our meetings will be full, saints will be revived and sinners will be converted. This can only come from the Lord’s mercy; but it will come, and we are called to expect it. The time, the set time, has come. Let’s rouse ourselves. Let’s love every stone of our Zion, even if it has fallen down. Let’s treasure the least truth, the least ordinance, the least believer, even though some may despise them as so much dust. When we favor Zion, God is about to favor her. When we take pleasure in the Lord’s work, the Lord himself will take pleasure in it.

notes.note: The hill in Jerusalem where the temple stood; here a picture of the church.
God’s appointed time.

notes.term: Take pleasure in her stones, and favor the dust thereof
notes.note: The exiles loved even the rubble of ruined Jerusalem ([[Ps.102.14|Psalm 102:14]]).

notes.term: There’s not a lamb in all thy flock
notes.note: From Philip Doddridge’s hymn “Do not I love thee, O my Lord?” Disdain means scorn.
“Repent ye therefore… when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord” ([[Acts.3.19|Acts 3:19]]).
Rouse ourselves to action.
A practice Christ gave the church, such as baptism or the Lord’s Supper.

modern: Yes, Lord, we believe it: we will never die. Our soul may be separated from our body, and that is a kind of death; but our soul will never be separated from God, which is the true death, the death threatened against sin, the death penalty that is the worst thing that can happen. We believe this most firmly, for who will separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord? We are members of the body of Christ; will Christ lose parts of his body? We are married to Jesus; will he be bereaved and widowed? It isn’t possible. There is a life within us that can’t be cut off from God; yes, and the Holy Spirit lives within us, so how can we die? Jesus himself is our life, and so there is no dying for us, for he can’t die again. In him we died to sin once, and the death sentence can’t be carried out a second time. Now we live, and live forever. The reward of righteousness is everlasting life, and we have nothing less than the righteousness of God, so we can claim the very highest reward.
Living and believing, we believe that we will live and enjoy. So we press forward in full assurance that our life is safe in our living Head.

notes.term: Whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die
notes.note: Jesus to Martha, before he raised her brother Lazarus ([[John.11.25-John.11.26|John 11:25–26]]).

notes.term: The death which was threatened to sin
notes.note: “For in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die” ([[Gen.2.17|Genesis 2:17]]); “the wages of sin is death” ([[Rom.6.23|Romans 6:23]]).

notes.term: Who shall separate us from the love of God
Members of the Body of Christ
notes.note: “Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular” ([[1Cor.12.27|1 Corinthians 12:27]]).
Robbed by death of someone loved.
The death sentence.

notes.term: In Him we died unto sin once
notes.note: “For in that he died, he died unto sin once: but in that he liveth, he liveth unto God” ([[Rom.6.10|Romans 6:10]]).
“And he is the head of the body, the church” ([[Col.1.18|Colossians 1:18]]).

modern: The godly are tempted and tried. Faith that is never put to the test isn’t true faith. But the godly are rescued from their trials, and not by chance or by lesser means, but by the Lord himself. He personally takes on the work of rescuing those who trust him. God loves the godly, the godlike, and he makes a point of knowing where they are and how they are getting on.

Sometimes their way seems a maze, and they can’t imagine how they will escape the danger that threatens them. What they don’t know, their Lord knows. He knows whom to deliver, when to deliver and how to deliver. He delivers in the way that is best for the godly, most crushing to the tempter and most glorifying to himself. We can leave the “how” with the Lord, and be content to rejoice that, in some way or other, he will bring his own people through all the dangers, trials and temptations of this mortal life to his own right hand in glory.
Today it isn’t for me to pry into my Lord’s secrets, but to wait patiently for his time, knowing this: though I know nothing, my heavenly Father knows.

notes.term: The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly
notes.note: Peter’s conclusion after the examples of Noah and Lot, rescued while the wicked were judged ([[2Pet.2.5-2Pet.2.9|2 Peter 2:5–9]]).
The ordinary means and helpers God works through.
Task, duty.
A maze.
“For your heavenly Father knoweth that ye have need of all these things” ([[Matt.6.32|Matthew 6:32]]).

modern: See the protecting power of trust in God. The great men of Jerusalem fell by the sword, but poor Ebed-melech was safe, for his confidence was in Jehovah. Where else should a man trust but in his Maker? We are foolish when we prefer the creature to the Creator. Oh, that we could live by faith in everything; then we would be rescued in every time of danger! No one ever trusted in the Lord in vain, and no one ever will.

The Lord says, “I will surely deliver thee.” Notice the divine “surely.” Whatever else may be uncertain, God’s care for believers is sure. God himself is the guardian of the gracious. Under his sacred wing there is safety even when danger is everywhere. Can we accept this promise as sure? Then in our present emergency we will find that it stands firm. We hope to be rescued because we have friends, or because we are careful, or because we can see hopeful signs; but none of these things is half as good as God’s simple “because thou hast put thy trust in me.” Dear reader, try this way, and once you have tried it, you will keep to it all your life. It is as sweet as it is sure.

notes.note: The Ethiopian official who rescued Jeremiah from the cistern; God promised to spare him when Jerusalem fell ([[Jer.39.15-Jer.39.18|Jeremiah 39:15–18]]).

notes.term: Thy life shall be for a prey unto thee
notes.note: You will escape with your life, as a soldier carries off his plunder.
The personal name of God in the Old Testament, printed “the LORD” in most English Bibles.
“And worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator” ([[Rom.1.25|Romans 1:25]]).
“Under his wings shalt thou trust” ([[Ps.91.4|Psalm 91:4]]).
About, everywhere.
Careful, sensible.

modern: It’s a heavy burden? Roll it onto the Almighty. It is your burden now, and it crushes you; but when the Lord takes it, he will make nothing of it. If you are still called to carry it, “he will sustain thee.” It will be on him, not on you. You will be held up under it so well that the burden will be a blessing. Bring the Lord into the matter, and you will stand upright under what would bow you down by itself.

Our worst fear is that our trial might drive us from the path of duty; but the Lord will never allow this. If we are righteous before him, he won’t let our affliction move us from where we stand. In Jesus he accepts us as righteous, and in Jesus he will keep us so.

What about this present moment? Are you going out to today’s trial alone? Are your poor shoulders to be rubbed raw again by the crushing load? Don’t be so foolish. Tell the Lord all about your grief, and leave it with him. Don’t cast your burden down and then pick it up again; roll it onto the Lord, and leave it there. Then you will walk free, a joyful, unburdened believer, singing the praises of your great Burden-bearer.

notes.note: Being all-powerful.
Allow.
Rubbed sore, as a harness rubs a horse.
Walk free. “And I will walk at liberty” ([[Ps.119.45|Psalm 119:45]]).
